issues.legal_issue: A Letters Patent appeal governed by a High Court rule prescribing a longer filing period is timely when filed within that period, notwithstanding the shorter period in the Limitation Act.
material_facts: The government appealed to a division bench from a single judge’s judgment in the High Court’s original jurisdiction.
A High Court rule allowed 30 days for the appeal, while the Limitation Act prescribed 20 days.
The appeal was filed within the period allowed by the High Court rule.
issues.conclusion: The High Court rule was a special law within section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, so the appeal was timely under the 30-day period and was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, a special or local law prescribing a different limitation period governs the covered appeal as if that period were prescribed in the First Schedule; accordingly, the rule made under clause 27 of the Letters Patent prevailed over Article 151. The Court approved Punjab Co-operative Bank Ltd. v. Official Liquidators, Punjab Cotton Press Company Ltd. (AIR 1941 Lahore 57).

predicates.letters_patent_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal under the Letters Patent from a single judge’s decision to a division bench of the same High Court.
predicates.high_court_rule_sets_longer_period: A rule of the High Court prescribes a filing period for that type of appeal that is longer than the period in the general limitation schedule.
predicates.filing_within_rule_period: The appellant filed the appeal within the period prescribed by the High Court rule.

issues.definition: When a Letters Patent appeal is governed by a High Court rule prescribing a longer period and is filed within that period, the appeal is timely.

issues.legal_issue: Property requisitioned for a limited authorized purpose must be released when that purpose has ceased and the property is being used for a different purpose.
material_facts: The government requisitioned a building under emergency rules for specified purposes and continued the requisition under a later enactment.
The building was later used for a private dance and music school rather than for any of the purposes for which it had been requisitioned.
The owners sought return of the building through a proceeding for release of the requisitioned property.
issues.conclusion: The original requisition purpose had ceased, so the owners were entitled to the property’s release and return of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 75-A of the Defence of India Rules limited requisition to the purposes specified in that rule, and the authority to use or deal with requisitioned property was confined to those purposes. Section 3 of the Requisitioned Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1947 continued the requisition but did not enlarge the authorized purposes. Under section 24(2) of the Requisitioning and Acquisitioning of Immovable Property Act, 1952, the existing requisition was deemed to be one under section 3 of that Act; the fiction did not validate an unlawful use or replace the original purpose with a different one. The proviso to section 6 required release when the purpose for which the property was being used ceased to exist. The Court treated The State of Bombay v. Ali Gulshan ([1955] 2 SCR 867) as not determining the criterion in this case and did not express an opinion on the broader contention based on it.

rule.if: release_request_proceeding and requisitioned_for_limited_authorized_purpose and requisition_continued_under_later_law and current_use_outside_original_purpose

predicates.release_request_proceeding: The proceeding seeks release and return of property that remains under requisition.
predicates.requisitioned_for_limited_authorized_pur: The property was requisitioned under an authority that permitted requisition only for specified purposes.
predicates.requisition_continued_under_later_law: A later law continued the existing requisition without enlarging the purposes for which the property could be used.
predicates.current_use_outside_original_purpose: The property is being used for a purpose outside those for which it was originally requisitioned.

issues.definition: When a release proceeding concerns property requisitioned for limited purposes, the requisition was continued without expanding those purposes, and the current use falls outside them, the government must release the property.
